An inverse dose-response relationship was observed between physical activity (PA) and both breast cancer-specific and all-cause mortality, with significant reductions in hazard ratios noted at 10-15 MET-hours per week of activity. 2. Higher levels of physical activity, both before and after a cancer diagnosis, were associated with improved survival outcomes across at least 11 different cancer types. This supports the global promotion of physical activity guidelines for cancer patients. 3. A systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effectiveness of aerobic exercise in hypertensive populations. Data from 14 studies involving 860 participants showed that aerobic exercise significantly improved blood pressure and heart rate. However, further well-designed studies are needed to confirm the optimal duration of exercise for these benefits. 4. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) and moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) were compared for their effects on blood pressure in adults with preto established hypertension. Both methods provided comparable reductions in resting blood pressure, but HIIT showed greater improvements in maximal oxygen uptake (VO2 max). Future studies should explore the efficacy of HIIT for reducing ambulatory blood pressure. 5. Resistance training alone was found to reduce both systolic and diastolic blood pressure in prehypertensive and hypertensive individuals. This supports the recommendation of resistance training as a management tool for systemic hypertension. 6. Tai Chi was shown to effectively improve blood glucose and HbA1c levels in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Long-term adherence to Tai Chi was associated with better glycemic control. 7. A meta-analysis comparing HIIT and MICT in individuals with prediabetes and T2DM found that both exercise modalities induced similar cardiometabolic adaptations. However, HIIT provided greater benefits to functional capacity, as measured by VO2 max, in T2DM patients. 8. Exercise interventions significantly improved glycemic control in Korean patients with non-insulin-treated T2DM, although they did not significantly reduce body weight. Aerobic training was particularly beneficial for this population. 9. Tai Chi and Qigong interventions showed potential for reducing major stroke risk factors, such as hypertension and hyperlipidemia, but no trials directly examined their effects on stroke incidence. More robust studies are needed to confirm their efficacy and safety. 10. Resistance training improved glycemic control, muscular strength, and lean body mass in elderly patients with T2DM. High-intensity resistance training may be a viable strategy for managing T2DM and age-related sarcopenia. 11. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined the effects of exercise on risk factors for diabetic foot ulcers, including glycated hemoglobin, peripheral arterial disease, and diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Aerobic, resistance, and combined exercise modalities were analyzed, with combined exercise showing the most significant benefits.
